name: Southern Vietnamese Bánh Xèo
imageAlt: Vietnamese bánh xèo, a thin crisp rice-flour pancake folded around savory filling
imageCredit: Photo: DuyTran16, Wikimedia Commons, public domain.
summary: Southern Vietnamese bánh xèo with a thin turmeric rice-flour and coconut batter, pork, shrimp and bean sprouts cooked until audibly crisp and served with herbs, lettuce and nước chấm.
lead: The name promises the technique: batter should sizzle the instant it hits the pan, then cook into a brittle-edged yellow pancake wrapped around pork, shrimp and sprouts.
about: Bánh xèo are Vietnamese savory rice-flour pancakes whose name refers to the sizzling sound of batter meeting a hot pan. Versions differ significantly around Vietnam. SBS sources describing southern and Saigon-style bánh xèo emphasize a larger pancake, turmeric in the batter, coconut, pork or seafood, bean sprouts, fresh herbs and a fish-sauce dipping sauce. This recipe is therefore framed specifically as a southern-style home version rather than as a single national formula.
story: Vietnamese cooks and food writers describe bánh xèo as both street food and a highly social dish because the crisp pancake is commonly broken into pieces, wrapped in lettuce and herbs, then dipped in nước chấm. Regional distinctions matter: central Vietnamese forms can be smaller and differently seasoned, while southern examples are often broad, turmeric-yellow and coconut-enriched. The dramatic sizzle is more than a name; it signals that the pan is hot enough to drive moisture from the batter quickly and create the brittle lace that separates good bánh xèo from a soft crepe.
caveat: This is a southern Vietnamese adaptation. Bánh xèo varies by region, household, filling and batter; do not treat coconut milk, pancake size or this exact pork-and-shrimp combination as universal throughout Vietnam.
prepNotes: Give the rice-flour batter about 30 minutes so the flour fully hydrates. Stir before every pancake because rice flour settles quickly.
A quiet pour produces a soft pancake. The batter should hiss immediately and race across a thin film of hot oil.
A modest amount of pork, shrimp and sprouts lets steam escape and gives the bottom enough contact with the pan to become crisp.
ingredients: 1 1/4 cups cold water, plus 2 to 4 tbsp if needed
8 oz pork belly or pork shoulder, sliced very thin
8 oz medium shrimp, peeled, deveined and halved lengthwise if large
1/2 small yellow onion, very thinly sliced
1 head soft lettuce, leaves separated, for serving
1 cup mixed mint, Thai basil, cilantro and perilla leaves, as available
1 small red chile, thinly sliced, optional
steps: Whisk rice flour, cornstarch, turmeric and salt. Add coconut milk and 1 1/4 cups cold water and whisk until smooth, then stir in scallions. Rest 30 minutes. Meanwhile whisk fish sauce, lime juice, sugar, warm water, garlic and chile until the sugar dissolves; set the nước chấm aside.

Heat a 9- to 10-inch skillet over medium-high until a drop of water skitters and evaporates almost immediately. Add 1 teaspoon oil, then a few slices of pork and onion. Cook 60 to 90 seconds until the pork loses its raw surface and the onion smells sweet; add 2 to 3 shrimp pieces and cook just until their edges begin turning opaque.

Stir the batter from the bottom. Pour about 1/3 cup around the outer edge of the hot pan while tilting and rotating rapidly so it runs into a very thin layer. The pour should produce a loud, immediate sizzle. If the batter sits thickly without hissing, increase the heat before the next pancake.
Cover for 90 seconds to set the top, then uncover and scatter about 1/3 cup bean sprouts over one half. Drizzle 1 teaspoon oil around the rim and continue cooking uncovered 3 to 5 minutes.

Checkpoint: the outer edge should visibly lift and look dry and brittle, the underside should be deep golden rather than pale yellow, and the center should no longer look wet. Shake the pan; a properly crisp pancake should release with little resistance.

Fold the empty half over the filling and slide the bánh xèo onto a plate. Keep it uncovered so escaping steam does not soften the crust. Repeat with remaining batter and filling, wiping out any scorched bits and restoring the pan to high heat between pancakes.

Serve immediately with lettuce, herbs and nước chấm. Tear off a crisp section, wrap it with herbs in lettuce and dip. The ideal bite should combine a brittle edge, tender rice-flour center, juicy filling and cool aromatic greens.
sources: SBS Food - Bánh Xèo by Adam Liaw

name: Ghanaian Red Red with Fried Plantain
imageAlt: Ghanaian red red bean stew; the photographed serving includes fish as a common accompaniment while this base recipe is meatless
imageCredit: Photo: benketaro, Wikimedia Commons/Flickr, CC BY 2.0. The photographed serving includes fish; the base recipe below follows a meatless red red preparation with fried plantain.
summary: Ghanaian red red: black-eyed peas simmered in a concentrated tomato, ginger, chile and red-palm-oil sauce, served with sweet fried ripe plantain and optional gari.
lead: Black-eyed peas become one of Ghana's most recognizable comfort foods when they are folded into a brick-red palm-oil and tomato stew and paired with caramelized ripe plantain.
about: Red red is a Ghanaian black-eyed pea stew strongly associated with red palm oil, tomato and chile and commonly served with fried ripe plantain. Ghanaian chef and writer Zoe Adjonyoh publishes a meatless version built from black-eyed beans, sustainable palm oil, onion, ginger, Scotch bonnet and tomato, while noting that the dish is eaten through the day. This home recipe follows that structure and uses canned beans as Adjonyoh explicitly permits, keeping the defining red palm oil rather than replacing it with a neutral oil.
story: The repeated name is commonly explained through the dish's color: red palm oil and tomato produce the deep red-orange stew, echoed by the golden-red surface of fried ripe plantain. Contemporary Ghanaian accounts describe red red as inexpensive, filling everyday food found in homes, canteens and street-food settings, often finished with gari and sometimes fish. Rather than making fish mandatory, this page centers the bean stew and plantain combination documented by Ghanaian cooks and treats fish as one possible accompaniment.
caveat: Red palm oil is a defining flavor and color here; ordinary vegetable oil will produce an edible bean stew but not the same red red. Fish, gari, avocado and other accompaniments vary, so they are presented as options rather than universal requirements.
prepNotes: Look for food-grade West African red palm oil with a fresh, nutty aroma. Rancid palm oil will taste waxy or stale.
Let the tomato base truly reduce
The sauce should lose its raw tomato smell and show small beads of red oil at the edges before the beans go in.
Yellow plantains with black spotting caramelize and give the sweet contrast expected beside the savory beans; green plantains stay starchy.
ingredients: 2 (15 oz) cans black-eyed peas, drained and rinsed
1/2 Scotch bonnet chile, seeded and minced, plus more to taste
1/2 tsp Ghanaian or West African-style curry powder, optional
1 (14.5 oz) can crushed or finely chopped tomatoes
3/4 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
2 large ripe plantains, yellow with black spots
1/2 cup gari (toasted cassava granules), optional for serving
steps: Warm the red palm oil in a heavy saucepan over medium heat until fluid and shimmering but not smoking. Add onion, ginger, Scotch bonnet and chile flakes. Cook 5 to 7 minutes, stirring, until the onion is soft and the raw ginger aroma has mellowed.
Stir in curry powder if using and tomato paste. Cook 2 minutes, scraping the bottom, until the paste darkens slightly and smells sweet rather than metallic.
Add canned and fresh tomatoes, salt and pepper. Bring to a brisk simmer, then reduce to medium-low and cook uncovered 15 to 20 minutes, stirring regularly.

Checkpoint: the tomato base should be thick enough that a spoon dragged across the pot leaves a brief trail, its raw acidic smell should have softened, and small red-orange beads of palm oil should appear around the perimeter.

Fold in the black-eyed peas and 1/4 cup water. Simmer 10 to 12 minutes, adding another splash of water only if the stew begins sticking. Mash about 1/2 cup of the beans against the side of the pot and stir them back in for body.

While the beans simmer, peel the ripe plantains and cut them on the diagonal into 1/2-inch slices. Heat about 1/4 inch neutral oil in a skillet over medium-high. Fry in batches 2 to 3 minutes per side until deep golden with caramel-brown edges; drain on a rack or paper towels.
Final checkpoint: the beans should be creamy inside but mostly intact, the sauce should cling rather than pool, and the palm oil should smell nutty, not raw or burnt. Adjust salt and chile.
Serve the red red hot with fried plantain and a spoonful of gari if desired. Fish or avocado can be added at the table, but the bean-and-plantain base stands on its own.
sources: Zoe's Ghana Kitchen - Red Red Vegan Bean Stew

name: Dominican Mangú with Vinegar Onions
imageAlt: Dominican mangú, a smooth mash of boiled green plantains
imageCredit: Photo: Ll1324, Wikimedia Commons, CC0 1.0 public-domain dedication.
summary: Dominican mangú with very tender green plantains mashed smooth with butter and water, then topped with warm red onions sharpened with vinegar.
lead: Mangú turns green plantains soft and creamy rather than crisp, then cuts their richness with red onions warmed just enough to keep a little bite and sharpened with vinegar.
about: The Dominican Republic's official tourism site recommends mangú as a traditional breakfast of boiled and mashed green plantains, commonly served with eggs, fried cheese and fried salami. Dominican food writer Clara González documents the same core technique: boil green plantains until very tender, mash them immediately with butter or oil and water, and top with red onions warmed with vinegar. This recipe focuses on that mangú-and-onion foundation; the full breakfast combination known as los tres golpes is offered as a serving option, not built into the mash itself.
story: Plantain mashes across the Caribbean reflect centuries of African, Indigenous, European and Atlantic food exchange, but mangú has a specifically Dominican place at the breakfast table. What distinguishes the texture is aggressive mashing while the plantains are hot and the addition of enough water to make the purée looser than seems necessary at first. Dominican cooks note that mangú tightens quickly as it cools. Vinegar-bright red onions provide the characteristic contrast, while fried egg, queso de freír and Dominican salami can turn the plate into los tres golpes.
caveat: Use green, unripe plantains for classic savory mangú; yellow plantains will make a sweeter, softer mash. Butter, olive oil and historically lard all appear in Dominican practice, so the butter used here is a documented modern choice rather than the only legitimate fat.
prepNotes: The peel should be fully green and the flesh firm. Riper fruit changes both sweetness and texture.
Plantain starch firms as it cools. Have butter and room-temperature water ready before draining so you can work while the pieces are steaming hot.
Make it slightly looser than you want
Mangú thickens between pot and table. Stop when it looks a little softer than the final consistency you prefer.
ingredients: 2 tsp kosher salt, divided, plus more to taste
6 tbsp salted or unsalted butter, softened, or olive oil
1 to 1 1/2 cups room-temperature water, added gradually
1 large red onion, halved and thinly sliced
2 tbsp apple cider vinegar or other mild fruit vinegar
Fried eggs, queso de freír and Dominican salami, optional for serving as los tres golpes
steps: Trim the ends from the green plantains. Score each peel lengthwise along a ridge without cutting deeply into the flesh, then pry away the thick peel. Cut each plantain into 4 pieces.
Place plantains in a pot, cover with water by at least 1 inch and add 1 1/2 teaspoons salt. Bring to a boil, then maintain a steady simmer 18 to 25 minutes depending on size and freshness.

Checkpoint: a fork or thin knife should slide through the thickest piece with almost no resistance and the center should look uniformly pale and starchy, with no hard chalky core. Undercooked plantain produces stubborn lumps.

While the plantains cook, warm olive oil in a skillet over low heat. Add red onion and remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt and cook 3 to 5 minutes until heated and slightly softened but still visibly crisp. Stir in vinegar, let it hiss for 20 seconds, then remove from the heat. The onions should smell sharp and fruity, not deeply caramelized.
Drain the plantains and begin mashing immediately with a sturdy fork or potato masher. Beat in the butter, then add 1 cup room-temperature water gradually while continuing to mash and fold.

Checkpoint: the mangú should become smooth, glossy and softer than mashed potatoes, with few to no lumps. If it stands in a stiff mound, beat in more water 2 tablespoons at a time; it will tighten as it sits.
Taste for salt and spoon onto warm plates right away. Top generously with the vinegar onions and some of their oil.

Serve as-is or add fried eggs, queso de freír and Dominican salami for the breakfast combination commonly called los tres golpes. If the mangú sits before serving and becomes firm, beat in a splash of warm or room-temperature water to restore its creamy texture.
sources: Dominican Republic Ministry of Tourism - official FAQ on traditional Dominican breakfast
